720: I hand out cards all night. I keep exactly none of them. It is a very generous job.
721: People sit down sure of themselves. They stand up humble. I mostly just make sure nobody eats the chips.
722: One man won everything, said thank you, and left forever. Smartest person I have ever met.
723: I have watched grown adults blow on dice like it changes the tiny numbers inside. It does not.
724: My whole job is spinning a wheel and pretending I know where it stops. I never do.
725: I have seen every lucky face and every unlucky face. They look the same. Just at different times.
726: I stand still for eight hours and move only my hands. My feet have forgotten what we do here.
727: A woman kissed her coins for luck before every bet. The coins remained coins. She kept kissing them.
728: People trust me with everyone's money and none of it is ever mine. I have stopped minding this.
729: I shuffle cards so much my hands do it while I sleep. My family finds this alarming.
730: The rule is I take no sides. So I cheer for absolutely no one, very quietly, all night long.
731: Someone asked me for a winning strategy. I told them the exit is that way. That is the strategy.
732: I have watched fortunes come and go across this little table. Mostly go. Almost always go.
733: I say the same three sentences all night. By closing time they have stopped meaning anything.
734: A boy asked if the wheel was magic. I said no, it is just very round. He was disappointed.
735: I hand chips out, then I gather them back. The pile is exactly the same size at dawn as at dusk.
736: My table has seen more tears than a sad wedding. And more hats. So many strange hats.
737: I never gamble myself. I have watched what happens. I go home, I make soup, I sleep fine.
738: People think I control the luck. I control a wheel and a small stick. That is my entire power.
739: A child waved at me for an hour instead of playing. Honestly the best customer I ever had.
740: The morning train was forty seconds late. I have not recovered, and I will not pretend I have.
741: I have memorized the whole timetable. Ask me anything. Please. Nobody ever asks me anything.
742: My job is to make trains leave on time. The trains do not always share this dream with me.
743: I ring the bell, I wave the little flag, the train goes. It is a small ceremony. I take it seriously.
744: A clock that is one minute wrong keeps me awake. I know how that sounds. I have accepted it.
745: People run for trains and miss them. I stand very still and catch every single one. Every day.
746: I have a whistle and the authority to use it. I use it exactly on schedule, never one second early.
747: Somebody asked when the next train comes. I told them the exact minute. They looked frightened.
748: The timetable is a promise. I did not write it, but I have decided to defend it with my life.
749: I wave goodbye to strangers all day long. None of them wave back. The trains do, sort of.
750: I keep this platform swept, straight, and on time. It is the tidiest thing in my entire life.
751: A late train is a small tragedy. A train that arrives early is somehow worse. Do not ask me why.
752: Thousands leave and never return. I have started taking it a little personally, which is unreasonable, I know.
753: I point at the big clock a lot. It is the most important object here and it agrees with me.
754: The rule is simple. The train leaves when I say. The train, so far, has other opinions.
755: I stand on this platform in every kind of weather. The trains do not thank me. I do not expect it.
756: A child asked to hold my flag. I said absolutely not, then let them wave it once. Just once.
757: Everyone here is going somewhere far. My longest journey is to the end of the platform and back, twice a day.
758: I check the departure board four times an hour. It never changes. I check it anyway, to be sure.
759: My whole day runs on minutes. When one is wasted, I feel it personally. I feel it right here.
